title: The Seventh Night
subtitle: Saturday 21 to Sunday 22 October 1893: The Bones Under the Hearth, What the Fortune Owes, Fire in the Stone House, and Her Name Said in Her Room

setting.name: Greywick House, Haverkill and the Landing, the seventh night and the eighth morning
setting.description: The last day and the last night of the will, and the truth of the fortune. On Saturday the storm has gone, the river is high and brown, the bridge is down, and the house is full of people who have not slept. The party knows the four rules. What remains is to choose. Laying Sabina Roelofs needs her own key in her own door, her name said in her room by one of the Greywick blood, and what was taken given back in her hearing: the Landing, which is the half of the Greywick fortune that survived the Panic. The codicil said so; if it burned, Strick can swear to it, but only the heirs can do it now. Conrad's fifth is already owed to the railroad he robbed. Linus, if he lives, wants his father's wishes done. Honora and Ellis must decide what their shares are worth to them. Dory Oudekerk, a farm woman from Claverack, learns that she is the heir to a railroad terminus. And Leonora Greywick, at liberty in the house under the constable's eye because no one will lock her door, has one plan left: at two in the morning, with kerosene from the coach house, she fires the stone house to burn the bones and the room and the rite with them. If the stone house burns with the Juffrouw unlaid, she is loosed into all of Greywick House. On Sunday at nine, in the library, Strick reads the codicil, or swears to it, and the inheritance is divided among those who kept seven nights.
setting.atmosphere: After the storm: a washed blue sky, cold sun, branches down across the lawns, the river high and loud and carrying whole trees down to the sea, the Catskills sharp as cut paper. Everyone moves slowly and speaks quietly, as after a death. The house is very still. The lamp in the river window is the last it will ever need, if the players do this right. In the evening the cold comes back hard, a clear frost with a three-quarter moon on the river; at two, there is smoke. The tone of the finale is gothic and humane: the dead woman is a person to be given back what is hers, not a monster to be destroyed; the living woman is a person who did a monstrous thing; and the fortune is the thing the family must decide whether to keep. Let the rite be quiet and the fire be loud.

keyLocations.name: The Cellar Kitchen and the Hearthstone
keyLocations.description: The low vaulted kitchen of the stone house, with the eight-foot hearth, the bluestone hearthstone, the old bake oven, a pantry with a bolt on the inside, and the door from the main house's cellar passage. By Saturday the hearthstone may already be up (gw-scenario-002); if not, Mrs. Quell, turned, will help lift it.
features: The hearthstone and the shallow grave in the clay beneath
The sail she was wrapped in, rotted to lace, and a scrap of grey wool
The pantry and its inside bolt, where Gerrit slept in 1871
Oak beams overhead, dry as tinder after a hundred and sixty years over a kitchen fire
encounters: Mrs. Quell, Gerrit, Dr. Wyle and the Reverend at the lifting of the stone (no combat)
Leonora, at two in the morning, with two cans of coach-house kerosene (see Fire in the Stone House)
secrets: CLUE F5 (if not already found): the bones of a woman of about thirty, the back of the skull broken against stone, a hairpin in the right hand. Dr. Wyle (Medicine DC 12): she fell or was struck against the hearth's edge; she did not drown; she has lain here since the 1850s by the clay and the sail.

CLUE F6 (Mrs. Quell, at the graveside, if she has not said it): 'My father told me the night before he locked his door, in October of '53. I helped Mr. Abram with the Juffrouw. She tried the window and I pulled her back and she struck the hearth. We put her under the stone. Mr. Abram said she sailed on the Tuesday. God forgive me.' She will say it again to the constable and to Strick.

Moving the bones does not lay her and does not anger her. The Reverend will take them down the bluff path to the Old Stone Church in a plain box, by daylight, and bury them in the Roelofs row on Sunday afternoon under her own name, if the family pays for a stone. Doing it is a kindness, not a rite.

The beams: Ellis Callender (or Mechanics DC 12, or anyone who has fought a fire) sees at once that the cellar kitchen is the stone house's weak point: oak beams overhead, the stair above them, the river room above that. A fire set here takes the whole wing in twenty minutes.

keyLocations.name: The Library at Nine
keyLocations.description: The same long table where the will was read, by daylight this time, with the gasoliers dark and the river shining in the tall windows. Strick at the head with his dispatch box; the register, signed seven times by those who kept the nights; the household along both sides; Abram's portrait over the fire with its hand on the iron key.
features: The register, with its forfeits ruled through in Strick's hand
The codicil: whole, scorched, or ash in Leonora's grate
Abram's portrait: the iron key painted beside his hand, the same key the party now holds
encounters: The reading of the codicil, or Strick's sworn recital of it
Conrad's confession, if he makes one
Leonora, if she is still in the house and able to come down
secrets: CLUE F7 and H5 (the codicil, read or recited): Jasper's confession; the Landing yards, their railroad lease (worth $420,000 and paying $38,000 a year) and the river frontage to the heirs of Sabina Roelofs, being Dorothea Oudekerk of Claverack and her brothers Jan and Hendrick; an audit of the Haverkill & Berkshire's sinking fund; the house to Leonora for her life; and: 'my children are to open her door with her own key, and say her name in her room, and give back what we took, in her hearing, for I never could. I ask her pardon, and theirs, and yours.'

The division: under the will, the residue goes in equal shares to those of Leonora, Conrad, Linus, Honora and Ellis who kept all seven nights; anyone who forfeited (Linus, ruled absent on Sunday 15; anyone who went up the ladder) takes nothing. Strick says Linus's absence was 'not voluntary within the meaning of the will' and he will ask the Surrogate to restore his share; Conrad, to everyone's surprise, says he will not contest it. After the Landing and the Panic, each fifth is worth about $135,000; Conrad's is owed to the sinking fund.

If the codicil burned: Strick swears to its contents before the Surrogate at Poughkeepsie as a lost codicil, with Cyprian Tunstall (who witnessed it) beside him. It will take a year and probably succeed. Meanwhile the heirs can give the Landing back of their own will, by deed, and the GM should make that the stronger choice.

Leonora's life interest in the house: a person who murdered the testator cannot take under his will (a principle the New York courts were deciding that very decade). Strick knows it and says so, very quietly.

keyLocations.name: The River Room, the Seventh Night
keyLocations.description: The river room at night, as it was in 1852, opened with her key. Tonight nobody is kept in it: Linus is out, or dead. When the door opens, there is only Sabina Roelofs in her chair by the window with her back to the door, the rain on the glass, the fire laid and never lit, and the cold. This is where the rite must be done.
features: Her chair, her back, her wet hair
The lamp on the sill, lit by Mrs. Quell at dusk for the last time
The doorframe and its tallies, every set of them, and Linus's seven
The window: MIJN NAAM. GEEF TERUG written in frost
encounters: The Juffrouw (Bound Spirit), for the rite; she does not fight
Smoke coming up the stair, if Leonora's fire is not out
secrets: THE RITE (Rule 4, exactly): (1) her door opened with her own key from outside between midnight and dawn (the turner's WIS save DC 15) and held with iron; (2) her true name, Sabina Roelofs, spoken in the room by one of the blood that kept her: Honora, Linus, Conrad, or Ellis Callender, whose mother was Abram's daughter; not Leonora, not Dory, not anyone else, however brave; (3) what was taken given back in her hearing: the codicil read aloud and accepted by the Greywicks present, or a deed of gift of the Landing to her heirs signed in the room by a Greywick and handed to Dory Oudekerk or another heir of hers, or, failing paper, a Greywick's sworn word before witnesses in that room that the Landing will be returned, which the GM should accept only if the speaker means it and the table believes them. The leader of the rite makes an Occult check DC 15 (an Occultist has advantage, and Old Lore lets them speak the words for a Greywick who falters); on a failure, the words do not come in the right order this time, everyone in the room gains a point of Dread, and they may try again in an hour.

When the rite is done she stands up. Fear check DC 20 for everyone present: she turns round and looks at them, a square plain tired face, and her eyes go to Dory if Dory is there. She walks past them to the open door, and the people in the doorway find that they have stepped aside. On the threshold she stops and looks at the doorframe, at all the marks, and puts out her hand and touches the first seven, the fine ones low down. Then she goes down the stair, and the rain stops on the window, and the frost runs off the glass, and it is a dusty room with a lamp on the sill and the moon on the river. Laying a haunting: every character present drops to 0 Dread. Gerrit Brouwer sits down on the stair and cries.

Wrong rites, if the players try them first: burning the bones (she is not in the bones), reading the burial service over her (comfort, nothing more), salt, holy water, iron, destroying the box lock (the door will not break at night). Each costs a point of Dread to the one who tried. A Greywick speaking her name without giving anything back: she turns, looks at them, and is gone till tomorrow night. A gift that is not meant: nothing happens, and the speaker knows why.
If the stone house burns before the rite is done, the room is gone and she is loosed (see Fire in the Stone House).

keyLocations.name: The Old Stone Church and Haverkill Landing
keyLocations.description: Sunday afternoon in the village: the churchyard sloping to the river, the Roelofs row along the north wall with its gap after 1847, and below the hill the freight yards of the Haverkill & Berkshire, coal trestles and switch tracks and a red brick freight house, and at the end of them, the old stone pier where the Zwaluw tied up, cracked and weedy, with an iron ring still in it.
features: The gap in the Roelofs row, waiting
The river men's tablet inside the church: 'Captain Sabina Roelofs of the sloop Zwaluw'
The old stone pier and its iron ring
The railroad's freight house and the division superintendent's office, where the lease is filed
encounters: The Reverend Cornelis Vreeland, with a plain box and a spade
Mrs. Annetje Vedder, carried down Ferry Lane in a chair by two river men, with the Zwaluw's pennant
Dory Oudekerk on the old pier, looking at the yards and trying to understand that they are hers
secrets: The burial, if the players want it: the Reverend reads the service; Annetje Vedder speaks the river custom, the captain's name at the rail; a stone with a carved anchor costs $40 from the mason in Poughkeepsie, and Linus or Honora will pay. This is not part of the rite and does nothing to the house. It is the end of the story for Haverkill.

Dory's choice, if she is the heir: she can keep the lease with the railroad and be rich, sell the Landing back to the railroad outright for $400,000, or do what Sabina wanted and reopen the old pier as a free landing for the sloops and the farmers' boats alongside the railroad's yards, which the lease allows. Annetje, asked, says only: 'She'd have liked the pier.'

synopsis: The seventh night. The party knows the four rules and holds the key; what is left is the choice. On Saturday they lift the hearthstone if they have not, and Mrs. Quell tells what her father did. The heirs argue in the library over what the Greywicks owe: the codicil, whole or scorched or ash, gives the Landing, half of what the Panic left, to a farm woman from Claverack. Conrad confesses his theft. Linus, if he lived, wants his father's wishes done. Honora and Ellis must decide. Strick draws a deed of gift for any Greywick who will sign it. Leonora is at liberty in the house under Constable Mabie's eye, because nobody will lock a door on her, not even her. At dusk Mrs. Quell lights the river lamp for what may be the last time. At two in the morning Leonora slips the constable, takes two cans of kerosene from the coach house, bolts herself into the stone house's cellar kitchen and sets it alight, to burn the bones, the room and the rite. The fire is the house as a hazard: smoke up the north stair, oak beams going, the river room above. The party must break in, fight the fire or race it, decide whether to save the woman who set it, and get the rite done in the river room before the stone house burns: her key, her name in a Greywick's mouth, and what was taken given back in her hearing. If it is done, Sabina Roelofs stands, turns, looks at them, touches the first seven marks in the doorframe, and goes down the stair, and the house is only a house. If the stone house burns first, she is loosed into all of Greywick House, and it will keep one person every October until the family sells it. On Sunday at nine, in the library, Strick reads the codicil or swears to it; the inheritance is divided among those who kept seven nights; and in the afternoon, perhaps, a woman is buried under her own name in the Old Stone Church's yard with an anchor on her stone.
hook: Saturday, a little after eight, the library, the sun coming in across the long table. Strick has had the gas lit anyway, from habit, and sits at the head with his dispatch box open and empty in front of him, or with four scorched pages laid out flat under a paperweight. He looks very old. 'Mr. Greywick asked me to read this tomorrow at nine,' he says. 'I shall. But I think the family had better hear now what it asks of them, because it cannot be done tomorrow at nine. It must be done tonight.' He takes off his spectacles and polishes them. 'He was not asking for money. He was asking someone to open a door.'

conclusions.conclusion: F. The whole truth of the fortune
clues: F5: the bones under the hearth (the cellar kitchen)
F6: Mrs. Quell's account of her father's confession (the cellar kitchen)
F7: the codicil, read or sworn to (the library)
F1: the forged deed in Liber 97 (gw-scenario-002)

conclusions.conclusion: H. How she can be laid, and by whom
clues: H5: the codicil: 'open her door with her own key, and say her name in her room, and give back what we took, in her hearing' (the library)
H1: the journal fragment: 'by our blood' (gw-scenario-002)
H3 and H4: MIJN NAAM. GEEF TERUG; 'terug, terug' (gw-scenario-003)

acts.title: Saturday: What We Took
acts.description: A day of choices in daylight. The point of this act is that laying the ghost costs the family the fortune's foundation, and the players are among the family or among its guests. Let the heirs argue. Let Dory hear it. Let Conrad confess. Let Strick explain the law. And let Leonora, under the constable's eye in the morning room, listen to all of it through the open door.
objectives: Lift the hearthstone and hear Mrs. Quell's account, if not already done
Hear the codicil (or Strick's recital) and decide what the Greywicks will give back
Get a Greywick ready to say her name in her room, and something to give back in her hearing
Decide what to do about Leonora, short of locking her in

scenes.name: Under the Hearth
scenes.description: If the stone has not been lifted, it is lifted now, by daylight, with Mrs. Quell holding the lantern and the Reverend reading a psalm. If it was lifted on Thursday, this scene is the Reverend's plain box and the carrying of her down the bluff path to the church, which can be done today, by daylight, and is safe. Mrs. Quell gives her account (CLUE F6). Dr. Wyle writes, for the constable, what killed her. Dory, if present, kneels by the grave for a long time. Nobody should make jokes, and the GM should let the players feel that this is the first time anyone has been kind to Sabina Roelofs in forty-one years.
scenes.readAloud: In the cellar kitchen of the stone house, under the hanging oak beams, the bluestone slab comes up with a groan and a breath of cold clay, and Mrs. Quell holds the lantern over the hole and does not look away. The Reverend Vreeland reads the psalm in Dutch, quietly, the old way, and his voice does not shake. She is very small. The sail they wrapped her in has gone to brown lace, and there is a scrap of grey wool, and a long iron hairpin still caught in the bones of one hand, the hand that scratched seven marks into the oak upstairs. Mrs. Quell sets the lantern down on the edge of the hearth and folds her hands. 'My father put her here,' she says. 'And I've lit her lamp for twenty-seven years to say I was sorry, and never once said it to her face.'

skillChecks.success: A woman of about thirty, strong-boned, the hands of someone who hauled rope all her life; the back of the skull broken by a fall against a hard edge, the hearth's, at the height of a woman falling backward from a window. She did not drown. She did not die quickly. Dr. Wyle writes it out and signs it, and this time writes the truth.
skillChecks.failure: Old bones and a broken skull; the rest is for a better doctor.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Quell tells it whole, to the constable and to Strick (CLUE F6), and signs Strick's paper. She asks only that her father's name be left off the stone.
skillChecks.failure: She tells it, but in pieces, and breaks down before the end; Strick has enough to swear to, and the constable takes her word.

skillChecks.success: Nothing changes in the house when the bones are lifted, and nothing will when they are buried. She is not in the bones; she is in the room, and in the doorframe, and in what was done. The rite is upstairs, tonight. This is only the decent part.
skillChecks.failure: You half expect the house to sigh, or the cold to lift. It does not.

scenes.name: What We Took
scenes.description: The family council in the library. The codicil (or Strick's recital) is read in full (CLUE F7, H5). Then the argument, and the GM should play every side fairly. The Landing is the half of the estate that survived the Panic: $420,000 and a lease that pays $38,000 a year. Giving it back leaves each fifth at about $135,000 rather than $220,000; it also makes Dory Oudekerk, who has never had more than $60 at once, one of the richest women on the river. Conrad, broken, confesses the sinking-fund theft in front of everyone and says his share, whatever it is, belongs to the railroad's bondholders; he will sign anything. Linus, if alive, says he will give back his own share of the Landing whatever anyone else does. Honora and Ellis, if NPCs, are torn and honest about it. Strick explains: the codicil, if it survives or is proved, gives the Landing back whatever the heirs want; but the rite needs it given back in her hearing, tonight, and a deed of gift signed by one Greywick in that room is enough, in his opinion, 'to satisfy the lady, if not the Surrogate'. He drafts one. Dory, if played, has the most interesting choice in the room: she can refuse it.
scenes.readAloud: Strick reads the codicil in the same dry careful voice he read the will, and it takes eleven minutes, and nobody moves. Jasper Greywick's confession, in Jasper Greywick's words: a deed she never signed, seven nights, a young man carrying trays to a locked door, a woman under a hearthstone, forty years of lamps and iron and silence. The Landing, the yards, the lease, the river frontage, to the heirs of Sabina Roelofs. An audit of the sinking fund; at that, Conrad shuts his eyes. And at the end, in a sentence Strick reads twice because his voice goes the first time: 'My children are to open her door with her own key, and say her name in her room, and give back what we took, in her hearing, for I never could. I ask her pardon, and theirs, and yours.' Strick folds the pages. In the silence the river shines in the windows, and the farm woman from Claverack sits with her big hands in her lap and stares at the lawyer as if he has spoken in a foreign language.

skillChecks.success: You carry the room. Linus first, then Conrad, then Honora and Ellis (or the players who are Greywicks), agree that the Landing goes back, by the codicil and by deed tonight, whatever the Surrogate later says. Strick draws the deed of gift on the library table and every Greywick present signs it. One will carry it into her room.
skillChecks.failure: The family splits: some will give, some will not. Strick draws the deed anyway, for any Greywick who will sign. One signature is enough for the rite, if it is meant. The rest is for the courts.

skillChecks.success: Through the open door to the morning room, Leonora sits with the constable and listens to every word. When Strick reads that she is to have the house for her life, she smiles very slightly. When Strick says, quietly, that a woman who killed her husband cannot take under his will, she stops smiling. She has one thing left, and she is thinking about it.
skillChecks.failure: The widow sits with the constable in the next room, very still, like a woman at a funeral.

skillChecks.success: Strick confirms what you remember from Liber 97 and the county clerk: Sabina Roelofs was never proved dead, her estate never administered, and her heirs, Marritje's line, have a claim to the Landing at law that the forged deed cannot defeat once the forgery is shown. The codicil only says what the courts would say anyway, given ten years and a good lawyer. The rite is the only part that cannot wait.
skillChecks.failure: Law, codicils, surrogates, deeds. Strick knows; you will have to trust him.

scenes.name: The Widow in the Morning Room
scenes.description: Leonora asks to speak to the party, or to one of them (the one who took the key, or Honora). Constable Mabie sits by the door. She does not plead. She explains: a doctor's daughter from Rhinebeck, a widower's second wife at thirty-two, twenty years of running a house where nobody locks a door, a husband who told her in September that he would give away the half of everything that was still worth anything because of a woman who died before she was born, and publish why. 'I did the only thing this house ever taught anybody.' She asks what they will do with her. The constable will hold her for the judge on Monday, in the house, unlocked; there is no lock-up in Haverkill that is not a room with a door. Insight DC 13: she has not given up. Perception DC 14 (later, at dusk): Jem says Mrs. Greywick asked him at four whether the coach house lanterns had been filled. They had. Two of the five-gallon kerosene cans are now missing from the coach house.
scenes.readAloud: The morning room is full of cold clear light and the smell of the chrysanthemums someone brought in from the frost. Leonora sits by the window in her mourning, perfectly composed, her hands folded, the chatelaine gone from her waist and nothing in its place, and the big constable sits by the door with his helmet on his knee, looking at his boots. 'I wanted to see you,' she says. 'You've been very clever. I wondered what it would be like to be found out, and it's very like being a girl again, sitting outside my father's surgery waiting to be told I'd done something wrong.' She turns her head and looks out at the river. 'He was going to give it away. All of it that's worth anything. And print the reason in the Advertiser. I'd have been the widow of the man who did that, in a house nobody would visit, with a fifth of nothing. I did the only thing this house ever taught anybody.' She looks back at you. 'What are you going to do with me? You can't lock me in. You know what happens.'

skillChecks.success: She is not asking for mercy. She is measuring you, as she measured everyone at the reading. She has a plan, still, and it is tonight, and it is the one thing left that can take the Landing back from Dory and the rite from the Greywicks: fire.
skillChecks.failure: A woman who has lost everything, being honest at last. Or something like honest.

skillChecks.success: Something you say reaches her: Linus, or Jasper, or the young man with the tray. For a moment the composure goes, and she says, 'I sat outside his door every night of that week. I heard him. I didn't open it,' and puts her hands over her face. If anyone can stop her tonight with words, it is now. (She will not set the fire; she will sit up in the hall with the constable all night and say nothing at all.)
skillChecks.failure: 'You sound like him,' she says. 'Go away now. I'm tired.'

skillChecks.success: You make it plain that she will be watched every minute until Monday. She believes you. She waits, all night, for someone to look away, and the GM should let the players decide whether anyone does; if they keep the watch, she never reaches the coach house, and the seventh night is the rite alone.
skillChecks.failure: She inclines her head politely and asks Jem for a pot of tea.

encounters: No combat by day. The bones, the codicil, the family and the widow.

acts.title: The Seventh Night
acts.description: Dusk, the last lamp, and then the long cold night with the rite at its end and, unless the players have watched Leonora every minute, the fire at two. The point of this act is to put the rite and the fire in the same building at the same time. The players can put the fire out and then do the rite in peace; they can do the rite first and let the stone house burn afterwards, a building and nothing more; or they can do both at once, which is the best and worst thing in the campaign.
objectives: Sign the register at sunset for the seventh time
Watch Leonora, or find the fire
Put out or survive the fire in the stone house; decide whether to save Leonora
Perform the rite in the river room: her key, her name, what was taken given back

scenes.name: The Last Lamp
scenes.description: Dusk, 5:10. Mrs. Quell carries the lamp up the north stair for the last time, if the rite succeeds, and asks if one of the family will carry it for her tonight. The register is signed. Dinner, a quiet one. The household agrees on the night: the rite at midnight or after (her key turns only between midnight and dawn); who goes in (a Greywick, the key-turner, someone with iron for the door, Dory if she will, an Occultist if there is one, the Reverend if asked); who watches Leonora. The GM should let the players plan this and then let something go slightly wrong: Constable Mabie, who has not slept for two nights, falls asleep in his chair in the hall at half past one, and the widow is not on the settle when he wakes.
scenes.readAloud: At ten past five the sun goes down behind the Catskills in a long bar of red over the river, and the cold comes up out of the ground at once, hard and clear, with a frost already silvering the branches the storm left on the lawn. In the hall the gas is lit. Mrs. Quell comes from the scullery with the brass lamp, newly trimmed and full of good oil, burning, and stops at the foot of the stairs. She looks at the family: at Linus wrapped in a rug by the fire if he is there, at Conrad, at the daughter, at the nephew, and at the farm woman from Claverack. 'Twenty-seven years,' she says. 'I'd like it if one of you carried it up tonight. It's your house. It was hers.'

skillChecks.success: Whoever carries the lamp up the north stair feels it: the stair is cold, and the river room's door is unlocked tonight, because nobody is kept, and inside it is only a dusty room at dusk; but at the threshold, for an instant, there is the smell of rain and the sense of someone waiting very patiently in a chair. She knows what tonight is. So does the house.
skillChecks.failure: A cold stair, a dusty room, a lamp on a sill. You set it down and come away quickly.

skillChecks.success: Planning the rite: her key, between midnight and dawn, from outside, with a steady hand; iron in the jamb; a Greywick to say her name in the room; the deed or the codicil read in her hearing, and handed to her heir if her heir is there. Nothing else. No salt, no prayers, no circles. Old Lore (an Occultist) recalls one more thing from the journal fragments: 'in her hearing' means aloud, in words she would understand. Say what was taken. Say the Landing.
skillChecks.failure: You have the shape of it. Whether you have it right, you will learn in the room.

skillChecks.success: At dusk, crossing the stable yard, you notice the coach house door ajar and two of the five-gallon kerosene cans gone from the shelf where Gerrit keeps them. Jem says Mrs. Greywick asked him at four whether the lanterns had been filled.
skillChecks.failure: The yard, the frost, the moon coming up. All quiet.

scenes.name: Fire in the Stone House
scenes.description: Two in the morning, unless the players have kept Leonora in sight every minute (in which case skip to The Rite). She went down the service stair with the kerosene at half past one while the constable slept, through the cellar passage into the stone house's cellar kitchen, and shot the old pantry bolt on the passage door behind her, so no one could stop her. She has soaked the beams and the stair foot and lit them. Smoke comes up the north stair and under the gallery door; the smell reaches the hall in five minutes. The fire is the house as a hazard (combat.json fire): it climbs the oak stair in ten minutes and reaches the river room's floor in twenty. Smoke: CON save DC 12 each minute in it or 1d6 poison damage and a level of exhaustion on a failure by 5 or more. The passage door is bolted from inside (Athletics DC 15, two may help, or the crowbar). Behind it Leonora is on the far side of the burning kitchen, by the hearth, with the empty cans, and the door has been bolted from inside with her behind it at night. She has called the Juffrouw on herself. The players can break in, fight the fire (Ellis Callender knows how: a bucket chain from the scullery pump, wet blankets, the garden hose from the gravity tank in the tower, close the doors to starve it; Mechanics or Athletics DC 13 for each ten minutes held), drag Leonora out or not, and decide whether to do the rite first.
scenes.readAloud: It is the smell first: lamp oil and woodsmoke, wrong, too much of it, coming down the gallery and into the hall where everybody sleeps, and then the sound, a soft roaring like a wind in a chimney when there is no wind tonight. The gallery door to the north wing is outlined in orange. When you get it open, smoke pours out of the stair in a grey wall, and up through it comes a red light from below and heat like an opened oven, and the old oak treads at the foot of the stair are burning. Down the cellar passage the door to the stone house's kitchen is bolted from the other side, and hot to the hand, and through it, over the roar, you can hear a woman's voice, quite calm, saying something you cannot make out, and another voice answering her in Dutch.

skillChecks.success: The bolt tears out and the door goes in, and the heat comes out at you. The kitchen is a cave of fire: beams alight, the stair foot blazing, the floor a lake of burning oil, and at the far end by the open hearth, standing over the grave, Leonora Greywick in her grey wrapper with an empty can at her feet, turning to look at you through the smoke. Fear check DC 15 (fire and her face). You can reach her: a dash through the fire (DEX save DC 13 or 2d6 fire damage, half on a success) and back carrying her.
skillChecks.failure: The door holds. It is very hot. Behind it the voices have stopped.

skillChecks.success: You fight it properly (advantage for a fireman): shut the gallery door to starve the stair, a bucket chain from the scullery pump, wet blankets on the treads, the garden hose run down from the tower's gravity tank, and the kitchen door shut again once Leonora is out. In twenty minutes the stone house is smoking, black, wet and standing, and the river room above it is untouched. Each ten minutes you hold it, the fire does not spread.
skillChecks.failure: It gets away from you: the stair goes, and the fire reaches the river room's floor beams. You have ten minutes left to do the rite before the room above is gone.

skillChecks.success: Leonora, carried out onto the frosted lawn, is burned on the hands and the face and choking on smoke, and she will live. She does not thank anyone. She looks up at the stone house against the stars and says, 'Is it still standing?' and when you say yes, she shuts her eyes.
skillChecks.failure: She is badly burned; she will live or die by morning, and it is not in your hands any more.

scenes.name: The Rite
scenes.description: The campaign's last scene in the house. Up the north stair (through the smoke, if the fire is not out), her key in her lock between midnight and dawn (WIS save DC 15), iron in the jamb, and into the river room as it was: the chair, her back, the rain, the frost writing. A Greywick says her name, Sabina Roelofs. The deed or the codicil is read aloud in her hearing (say the Landing), and given into Dory's hands if Dory is there, or laid on the sea chest if not. The leader makes an Occult check DC 15 (an Occultist has advantage). Then she stands, turns, looks at them (fear check DC 20), and walks out past them, and stops on the threshold to touch the first seven marks, and goes down the stair, through the smoke if there is smoke, and is gone. The rain stops. The frost runs. The room is a dusty room with a lamp on the sill and the moon on the river. Every character present drops to 0 Dread. If the fire has got away and the room is burning while they do it, run it as a race: each round in the room a CON save against smoke, and the floor going; the rite can be done in three rounds if no one falters.
scenes.readAloud: The iron key turns in the old lock with a sound like a bone, the door swings in, and it is raining in the room. The chair by the window. The wet dark hair. The grey dress and the pea jacket and the hands in the lap. The fire laid and never lit. On the glass, written in the frost, the two words you know by heart now. Someone from the family has to step forward, and does, and says her name aloud in her room for the first time in forty-one years: Sabina Roelofs. The woman in the chair goes very still, stiller than before, as if listening. Then the paper, read aloud, shaking, in the lamplight: the Landing, the pier, the wharves, the stone house, the four hundred acres of the bluff, given back. And she stands up. She is not tall. She turns round, and looks at you, a square plain tired face, wet with rain or something else; and her eyes go past the Greywicks to the farm woman from Claverack, and stay there a long moment. Then she walks to the door, and you find you have all stepped aside to let her pass.

skillChecks.success: The rite is done exactly as her rules ask. On the threshold she stops, and looks down at the doorframe, at all the rows of marks, and puts out one hand and touches the first seven, the fine ones low down, the ones she made. Then she goes down the stair, and the rain stops on the window, and the frost on the glass runs into water, and it is only a room. Gerrit Brouwer, on the landing, sits down on the top step with his cap in his hands and cries like a child. Everyone present drops to 0 Dread.
skillChecks.failure: The words come out in the wrong order, or the speaker's voice fails on the name, or the paper is read too fast to be heard. She does not stand. Everyone in the room gains a point of Dread. You may try again within the hour, if the room is still there.

skillChecks.success: The Greywick who speaks, speaks well: not just her name, but the truth, plainly, that Abram kept her here and took the Landing, and that Jasper carried her supper and did not open the door, and that they are sorry. (Advantage on the Occult check above. If Dory is there, she may speak too, in Dutch, her grandmother's name; the GM may let that be the thing that makes Sabina turn.)
skillChecks.failure: The words are right, and stiff, and frightened. They may still be enough.

skillChecks.success: (If the room is burning.) You hold your breath and your nerve through the smoke long enough for the words to be said and the paper read, and you get everyone out onto the stair behind her as the floorboards begin to glow.
skillChecks.failure: The smoke takes you (1d6 poison damage and a level of exhaustion); someone must drag you out; the rite must be finished by those still standing.

encounters: The fire in the stone house (combat.json fire): smoke CON saves DC 12 each minute; burning floor DEX save DC 13 or 2d6 fire; the stair goes in ten minutes, the river room's floor in twenty
Leonora in the burning kitchen (Frightened Townsman): she does not fight; rescuing her is a dash through fire
The Juffrouw (Bound Spirit) for the rite: she does not fight; fear check DC 20 when she turns

If the stone house burns with her unlaid: she is loosed, and every door in Greywick House closes at once (the hall is still safe until dawn); the GM runs the rest of the night as gw-scenario-003's doors, and the family sells the house within the year

acts.title: Sunday: Nine O'Clock
acts.description: The morning after. The point of this act is consequence: the codicil, the division, the widow, the Landing and the grave. Keep it short and let every player have a moment.
objectives: Hear the codicil read, or sworn to, at nine
See the inheritance divided among those who kept seven nights
Decide Leonora's fate with the constable
Bury Sabina Roelofs under her own name, if the players wish

scenes.name: The Library at Nine
scenes.description: Strick reads the codicil at nine exactly, or swears to it, as Jasper asked, though everyone has heard it; the register is closed and signed by Strick and Cyprian Tunstall; the forfeits are named. The division follows (see The Library at Nine, keyLocations). Conrad says what he did aloud, if he has not; Linus asks for the watch to be fetched from the crypt; Honora and Ellis (or the players) say what they will do with their shares. Dory, the heir to the Landing, is asked what she will do and should be given time to answer. Leonora is either in the morning room with the constable, burned and silent, or in the Poughkeepsie hospital, or dead in the stone house's kitchen. The constable takes Mrs. Quell's statement, Fanny's, Tuttle's, Linus's and Dr. Wyle's, and will take the widow to Judge Hallock on Monday. Nobody locks a door. End the scene with Abram's portrait: someone takes it down.
scenes.readAloud: Nine o'clock, Sunday, the library, the sun on the long table and the river shining beyond the tall windows, and every gasolier dark for the first time in a week. Mr. Strick opens his dispatch box at the first stroke of the hall clock, which Jem and Gerrit have stood up again in the night and which is going, a little slow, with a crack across its face. He reads the codicil one more time, for the record, because he was asked to, and nobody interrupts. Then he closes the register, signs it, has Cyprian Tunstall sign it, and takes off his spectacles. 'The seven nights have been kept,' he says. 'By most of us.' Over the fireplace Abram Greywick looks down at all of you with his hand on an iron key, and after a while Linus, or Honora, or somebody, gets up and lifts the portrait off its hook and turns it to face the wall.

skillChecks.success: The family agrees, in front of Strick and the constable, to everything the codicil asked: the Landing back, the audit, the confession printed in the Advertiser under Jasper's own name. Strick, who advised against it all, says it is the first time in forty years of practice he has seen a family do what a dead man asked of them because it was right.
skillChecks.failure: The family agrees to the codicil because the law will make them, and to nothing more. It is enough for the house; it is less than it could have been.

skillChecks.success: Dory Oudekerk is not thinking about money. She is thinking about the old stone pier, and her grandmother, and a woman with a square plain face who looked at her in a room full of rain. Ask her, and she will tell you what she means to do.
skillChecks.failure: The farm woman from Claverack sits in the corner and says nothing. She will need time.

skillChecks.success: Everyone in the house is exhausted, and almost all of them will be well in a week. Linus will walk by Wednesday. The fear is going out of the house: the north wing is cold only as stone houses are cold. (If the rite failed, it is not, and every player keeps their Dread.)
skillChecks.failure: Too many people, too little sleep. They will mend in their own time.

scenes.name: Her Name on a Stone
scenes.description: Sunday afternoon, the Old Stone Church, if the players want it: the Reverend Vreeland buries Sabina Roelofs in the Roelofs row by the north wall; Annetje Vedder is carried down Ferry Lane in a chair by two river men with the Zwaluw's pennant and says the captain's name at the graveside, the river way; Dory throws the first earth. The stone will come from Poughkeepsie in a month, with a small anchor carved after the name. Then, if the players like, down the hill to the Landing and the old stone pier with its iron ring. End the campaign there, or with the epilogue below.
scenes.readAloud: The churchyard slopes down toward the river in the cold bright afternoon, and the grave is open at the end of the Roelofs row, in the gap after 1847, and the box is very small. The Reverend reads in Dutch and then in English. Two old river men in their Sunday coats set down a chair, and in it a tiny bent woman in a white cap holds a faded blue-and-white pennant across her knees, and when the Reverend stops she lifts her face toward the river and says, in a voice that carries surprisingly far: 'Sabina Roelofs. Captain of the Zwaluw. Home.' Below the hill a freight engine shunts coal cars along the Landing, and its whistle goes, long and low, across the water to the Catskills and back.

skillChecks.success: Someone says a few words at the graveside, and says them well: who she was, what was done to her, that she is remembered. The village people who came out of curiosity stay to hear it, and go home and tell it, and by Christmas Haverkill knows the whole story and tells it right.
skillChecks.failure: Nobody can find anything to say. Annetje said it all.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Quell, at the back of the little crowd, has come down the bluff path on her own two feet for the first time in years; she does not come to the graveside, but she stays to the end, and on the way out she stops at a plain stone by the gate, Jotham Quell's, and stands there for a while, and then goes home.
skillChecks.failure: A small funeral for a woman forty-one years dead, on a cold Sunday.

skillChecks.success: The river is falling after the storm, and a sloop is coming down on the ebb with the wind behind her, an old Hudson River sloop with a gaff mainsail, one of the last on the river, and as she passes the Landing her skipper, who knows nothing about any of this, dips his flag to the church on the hill, the way the river men used to.
skillChecks.failure: The river, the hills, the cold sun. It is a beautiful day.

npcsInvolved.name: The Juffrouw (Sabina Roelofs, 1821 to 1852)
npcsInvolved.role: The bound one; to be laid
npcsInvolved.description: A square plain tired face, wet hair, a grey dress and a captain's pea jacket; seen at last when her name is said.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Her door opened, her name said in her room, what was hers given back in her hearing.

npcsInvolved.name: Leonora Greywick, 52
npcsInvolved.role: The widow; the murderer; the fire
npcsInvolved.description: Composed in the morning room, then in a grey wrapper in a burning kitchen.
npcsInvolved.motivation: One thing left: burn the stone house and the rite with it. Or, if reached by words in the morning room, nothing at all.

npcsInvolved.name: Dorothea 'Dory' Oudekerk, 30
npcsInvolved.role: Heir of Sabina Roelofs (a pregen; an NPC if not played)
npcsInvolved.description: A broad, quiet farm woman from Claverack with her great-aunt's face.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To know what happened to Sabina. Then, to decide what to do with a railroad terminus.

npcsInvolved.name: Linus Greywick, 31
npcsInvolved.role: The younger son, if he lived; the heir who wants his father's wishes done
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, wrapped in a rug, very clear-eyed.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Landing back, the door opened, his father's watch from the crypt.

npcsInvolved.name: Conrad Greywick, 38
npcsInvolved.role: The elder son; confessed or confessing
npcsInvolved.description: Sober, unshaven, smaller than he was on Sunday.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To pay back what he can and be done with lying.

npcsInvolved.name: Lemuel Strick, 64
npcsInvolved.description: With the codicil or without it; drafts the deed of gift on the library table.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see a dead man's wishes done, and the law satisfied after.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Judith Quell, 61
npcsInvolved.description: At the graveside of the woman her father killed, and then at his.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To say she is sorry to Sabina's face, once.

npcsInvolved.name: The Rev. Cornelis Vreeland, 53
npcsInvolved.role: Dominie; buries her under her name
npcsInvolved.motivation: To give a parishioner forty-one years missing a Christian burial.

npcsInvolved.name: Constable Gilbert Mabie, 48
npcsInvolved.description: Falls asleep at half past one. Mortified.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To bring the widow to Judge Hallock on Monday, alive.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Annetje Vedder, 88
npcsInvolved.role: Says the captain's name at the graveside
npcsInvolved.description: Carried down Ferry Lane in a chair, with the Zwaluw's pennant.

rewards.money: The inheritance. For each of Honora, Ellis, Linus and Conrad who kept seven nights, a fifth of the residue: about $135,000 if the Landing is given back, $220,000 if it is not (Conrad's goes to the sinking fund either way). The legacies are paid to everyone named who kept seven nights: Dr. Wyle $5,000, Mrs. Tierney $1,000, Cyprian Tunstall $500, Dory Oudekerk $1,000 and, if the codicil stands or the deed was signed, the Landing yards and their lease, worth $420,000 and $38,000 a year. Mrs. Quell $3,000 and the lodge; Gerrit Brouwer $1,000; a year's wages to every servant. Anyone who forfeited takes nothing under the will, but Linus or Honora will see them right.
items: The iron key of the river room, which opens nothing now; whoever turned it should keep it
Jasper's gold hunter watch, fetched from the crypt for Linus
The deed of gift, signed in the river room
Annetje Vedder's daguerreotype, given to Dory
A copy of the Haverkill Advertiser of 28 October 1893, with Jasper Greywick's confession printed under his name

twists: The rite needs a Greywick. If every Greywick in the house refuses, or is dead, the Juffrouw cannot be laid this year. She is still bound by her rules: the lamp, the iron, the key. The family can live with her, as Jasper did, or sell the house. Dory cannot do it for them, though she can stand in the room and say her grandmother's name.

Ellis Callender, the nephew, is a Greywick by blood through his mother, who was Abram's daughter and was cut off for marrying a fireman; he is the most likely player-Greywick to say her name, and the most likely to be fighting the fire at the same moment. Let him choose.

Leonora in the burning kitchen has bolted a door on herself at night. If the players leave her there, the Juffrouw may take her before the fire does, and she wakes in the river room as it was, and the rite will be done with her in it. The GM may decide that when Sabina stands and walks out, she passes Leonora on the floor without looking at her, and Leonora is found on the stair in the morning, alive, with nothing to say ever again about locked doors.

Dory may refuse the Landing. She is a farm woman with brothers and a mortgage and no wish to own a railroad yard. The rite only asks that it be given back in Sabina's hearing; what Dory does with it afterwards is hers, and Annetje will tell her the old pier would be a fine thing.

If the stone house burns with Sabina unlaid, the last scene is not a funeral but a sale: the family leaves Greywick House at Christmas, every door unlocked, a lamp burning in every window, and the new owner, a railroad man from New York, arrives in October.
dmTips: This is the finale. Budget an hour for Saturday, an hour and a half for the seventh night, and half an hour for Sunday. The fire and the rite can be run together; if your table likes a race, put the rite in a burning room; if it likes a quiet ending, let them put the fire out first.
Do not change the Juffrouw's rules now. If the players do exactly what Rule 4 says, she rests. If they do something else, nothing happens. That fairness is the point of the campaign.

Let the family argue about the money. It is a real choice: $85,000 a head, and a farm woman made rich. Do not make anyone who wants to keep it a villain; let them be people, as Leonora was until September.

Leonora's end is the players' choice. The rules give them a terrible option (leave her behind a bolted door) and the decent ones are harder. Honour whatever they choose, and show its weight on Sunday.
Fear checks: the fire and Leonora's face in it (DC 15); the river room (DC 20); Sabina turning (DC 20). After the rite, everyone present drops to 0 Dread. Say so, and describe the house going quiet.

If a player is Dory, give her the last word in the river room if she wants it. If a player is Honora, Linus's absence and Conrad's shame make her the family's voice. If a player is the Occultist, Old Lore is the moment to recall the exact words.

End with the epilogue: the following spring, the ice going out of the river, no lamp in the north window, and a stone in the Old Stone Church's yard with a name and a small carved anchor; or, if the rite failed, a lamp in every window of a house for sale.
